chunks.text: TL;DR
Every restaurant ends up needing the same dozen image sizes across G B P, Yelp, your site, social, OG, and menu thumbnails.
Shoot once at 30% above the recommended resolution. You can crop down; you cannot crop up.
A consistent angle on menu thumbnails matters more than camera quality. Mixed angles make the menu page read as broken.
Re-shoot twice a year. Photo cadence is one of the few maintenance loops that visibly affects average review rating.

Pull up the photo most operators upload as their hero: the dim phone shot of the dining room, taken at 7 PM under tungsten cans, portrait orientation because that’s how a phone sits in the hand. Now read it against the surface it landed on. The Google panel wanted 16:9 and cropped a grey-barred sliver out of the middle; the menu page wanted one consistent shape and got a portrait that broke the grid; the file was 1200 px on the long edge, so the hero looks soft and the thumbnail looks fine. Nothing is wrong with the room. Everything is wrong with the fit. This is a teardown of that photo, what the spec actually demands of it, row by row, and the one fix each row triggers.

Every restaurant ends up needing the same dozen image sizes, but almost no one shoots them at once. The result: a Google Business Profile cover that is the wrong aspect ratio and got cropped weirdly, a Yelp photo that is portrait when Yelp wants landscape, a menu page where every dish photo is a different shape and the layout breaks.

The spec sheet below is the document that closes that gap, the one I hand a photographer the morning of a shoot, or run myself off a phone. One shoot, the right specs decided in advance, and the result drops cleanly into every surface instead of getting cropped into one.
The 10 image sizes you actually need.

One shoot, ten outputs · the resolution rule. Shoot once, at 30% above max: You can always crop down. You can never crop up. (source). Site surfaces: Hero, interior banners, menu thumbnails, OG/Twitter card. (derivatives). G B P surfaces: Cover photo, profile, gallery, three different aspects. (derivatives). Social + Yelp: Yelp cover, Instagram square, Instagram portrait. (derivatives). One shoot, ten outputs · the resolution rule.

The ten surfaces a restaurant photo needs to ship to, with the aspect ratio and minimum resolution each one wants. Google Business Profile takes three of them: a sixteen-by-nine cover at twenty-one-twenty by eleven-ninety-two, a one-by-one profile badge at seven-twenty square, and a four-by-three gallery at ten-twenty-four by seven-sixty-eight, and you want thirty of those gallery shots in the first ninety days. Your own site takes two: a hero at twenty-one-by-nine or sixteen-by-nine, twenty-four-hundred by ten-twenty-four, and three-by-two interior banners at eighteen-hundred by twelve-hundred. Menu thumbnails are four-by-three or one-by-one at eight-hundred by six-hundred, pick one and use it consistently across every dish. Open Graph cards for shared links are one-point-nine-one to one, twelve-hundred by six-thirty. Yelp wants a three-by-one cover at fifteen-hundred by five-hundred. Instagram wants two formats: a one-by-one square at ten-eighty, and a four-by-five portrait at ten-eighty by thirteen-fifty, and the portrait is the one that actually gets seen in twenty-twenty-six.
My photo is not this aspect, what happens?

Center-crop. Anything past the left and right thirds disappears. If your subject, plate, person, signage, was framed against the edge, it gets clipped. Move the subject to the centre 60% of the frame before you shoot, or accept that the wings will be cropped.

Top and bottom get padded with whatever your background is, usually fine for plate-on-wood, ugly for room shots where the ceiling and floor are part of the story. Shoot 16:9 native if the surface needs it; up-conversion always reads as a hack.

The surface either rejects the upload or top-and-bottom letterboxes the photo. Yelp and G B P cover photos cropped from portrait look noticeably bad, cover sliver in the middle, grey bars top and bottom. Re-shoot. Phones default to 4:3 or 16:9 if you tap the aspect picker before the shot.
Crop in post. 4:3 → 16:9 takes a small slice off top-and-bottom; 4:3 → 1:1 takes a slice off the sides. Lightroom or Photos.app can both do batch aspect crops in under a minute for a 30-photo shoot.

That table is the artifact. Here is how to read it the way it gets used, not top to bottom as a reference, but as four lines the dim phone photo above failed, each one naming the single fix it triggers.

Aspect ratio, the line that crops you. The cover wants 16:9, the gallery 4:3, the menu thumbnail one shape held consistent, Instagram portrait at 4:5. The phone photo was portrait, so every landscape surface clipped it to a center sliver and every square one padded grey bars top and bottom. The fix this row triggers: tap the phone’s aspect picker before the shot, or frame the subject inside the centre 60% so the wings can be cropped without losing it.

Resolution, the line you can’t walk back. The largest surface on the list is the 2400 px site hero; the smallest floor is the 720 px G B P profile. The phone file was 1200 px, so it was already too small for the hero the day it was shot. The fix this row triggers: shoot at the top-of-list width plus 30%, because you can always crop down and you can never crop up.

File weight, the line nobody reads until the page is slow. The same hero ships to a phone over cell data and to a desktop on fibre, and the Jpg straight off the camera is heavier than either needs. The fix this row triggers: export site images as WebP at 80% quality before they ever touch the page.

Lighting, the line the camera can’t fix in post. The phone photo was shot at 7 PM under tungsten, which reads orange and dingy on a phone sensor no matter how good the phone is. The fix this row triggers: shoot 11 AM to 2 PM near a window; daylight is the one variable a better camera can’t buy back.
From the floor

The row I learned the hard way is the resolution one. Early on I shot a whole set on a phone in good light, loved how the dishes looked on the menu page, and only found the ceiling weeks later when I tried to pull one of those frames up as a site hero and it came out soft and pixel-thin. The light was right; the framing was right; the file was simply too small to crop up from, and there is no undo for that. Now the first thing I check before a shoot, before angle, before plating, is that the camera is set to its largest size. The thumbnail will always forgive you. The hero never does.
Resolution rules.

The pixel-width of the largest surface dimension a restaurant image needs to deliver, ranked. The site hero is the largest at twenty-four hundred pixels wide, twenty-one by nine aspect, the visual that defines the feel of the entire site. The Google Business Profile cover comes next at twenty-one hundred and twenty pixels, sixteen by nine, the hero of the panel. The Instagram square is next at one thousand and eighty pixels, used for grid posts. The G B P gallery sits at ten twenty-four pixels in four by three. The G B P profile circle and the menu thumbnails sit at seven hundred and twenty pixels and below. Shoot at the largest pixel-width on the list plus thirty percent, every smaller surface crops down from the same source. The shoot-once rule is a measurement, not a vibe.

Always shoot at the resolution recommended above Plus roughly 30% extra. You can always crop down; you can never crop up. A hero shot at 2400 times 1024 lets you also produce the 1200 times 630 OG card from the same file; a hero shot at 1200 times 630 leaves you stuck.
For images that ship to your site, export as C D N -friendly WebP at 80% quality, it is typically 60-70% smaller than Jpg without visible loss.
Alt text, the most-skipped part of the spec sheet.

Every image needs alt text . Not "IMG_4521.jpg," not the menu name, not "delicious food." A specific descriptive sentence: "Plate of carnitas with cilantro, white onion, and lime on a wood board." Costs 5 seconds per photo and earns you S E O + accessibility + AI-search citation.
For a 30-photo restaurant shoot, that is 150 seconds, or two minutes, of writing. Skip it and you have left every photo's S E O value on the floor.
So this is the artifact to put under the glass. Two versions of the same carnitas photo’s alt attribute, what a parser throws away on the left, what it keeps on the right:

A before-and-after of the alt-text attribute on the same carnitas photo, showing what Google's parser keeps and what it discards. The before version is the useless default: an alt value reading I M G underscore 4 5 2 1 dot J P G on one image, and a marketing line reading delicious food at our restaurant on the next. The filename names nothing, and Google strips the marketing language entirely, so the photo ranks for nothing and a screen-reader user hears noise. The after version follows the three rules the spec sheet teaches. Rule one, a specific subject: name the dish, plate of carnitas, not delicious food and not lunch. Rule two, a context noun: say where the photo is, with cilantro, white onion, and lime on a wood board, not just what is in it. Rule three, no filename and no marketing: describe, do not sell. The finished sentence reads plate of carnitas with cilantro, white onion, and lime on a wood board, and that one sentence earns the photo its S E O, its accessibility, and its AI-search citation for the five seconds it cost to write.
Alt text is the part of the spec sheet nobody reads. It is also the part Google reads first.
The shot list to hand a photographer.

Run Photo Brief . It generates a per-surface shot list with the spec sheet attached, exactly the document you would hand a photographer the morning of the shoot. Save the brief to your Workshop so you can re-run it for the next seasonal shoot.

The shoot itself is usually 2-3 hours for a 30-photo deliverable: the hero, 10-15 dishes, 4-6 room shots, 2-3 detail shots (a hand pouring wine, smoke off a grill, the chef plating). Done in one go, you have material for every surface for the next 12 months.
The 6-second pre-publish gut check.

Before any photo lands on the site, run it through this check. Six questions, one click each, takes about as long as it sounds. If you cannot answer "yes" to all six, the photo is not ready, not because the photo is bad, but because something around the photo is.

Six questions for any photo before it lands on the site. One: is the dish the sharpest thing in the frame? If not, it competes with whatever else is in focus. Two: was it shot in daylight, or at least with a daylight-balanced source? Restaurant overhead lighting reads orange and dingy on phone sensors. Three: are the edges clean? Garnish bleeding off the plate, a thumb in the corner, a stack of menus behind the dish, all visible at thumbnail size. Four: does the alt text name the dish specifically? ‘Plate of carnitas’, not ‘delicious food.’ Five: is it shot at three thousand pixels or more on the long edge so it can serve every surface from hero down to thumbnail? Six: is it less than six months old, or matching the current plating? If you can’t answer yes to all six, the photo isn’t ready, usually because something around the photo is wrong, not the photo itself.
The "shoot it yourself with a phone" version.

If hiring a photographer is not in budget, the phone version still works. Modern phones in good light routinely beat low-effort Dslr work, the variable that matters most is not the sensor, it is the time of day and the angle to the window. Three rules:
Daylight only. Shoot 11 AM to 2 PM near a window. Restaurant overhead lighting reads orange and dingy on the phone sensor.
One angle per dish, repeated. Pick top-down OR 3/4 front, and use the same angle for every dish so the menu page reads as one set.
Edit lightly. Increase exposure +0.3, boost shadows. Skip filters.

Shoot cadence · twice a year + menu changes. Pre-summer shoot: Memorial Day prep, patio, lighter dishes, daylight cocktails. (core set). Pre-holiday shoot: Mid-October prep, fall menu, warm tones, room shots. (core set). Menu pivot shoot: Any major menu change, new dishes, removed dishes, season swaps. (as needed). Shoot cadence · twice a year + menu changes.
How often to re-shoot.

Twice a year. Once before peak season (Memorial Day for summer, mid-October for the holidays); once when the menu changes substantially. If you re-shoot less than once a year, the photos start looking dated to regulars even if they are still technically accurate.

Save the dates in your Workshop alongside your Margin Math and Restaurant Audit scenarios. The compounding argument: photo cadence is one of the few maintenance loops that visibly affects average review rating, because the G B P cover and the menu thumbnails set the expectation guests bring through the door, and reviews are written against that expectation, not against the food alone.
Bad photos do not just fail to help. They actively drag the average down by setting the wrong expectation before anyone walks in the door.
Key takeaways
10 sizes cover every surface you actually need. Hand the spec sheet to your photographer with the brief.
WebP at 80% quality cuts file size 60, 70% vs Jpg, no visible loss.
Alt text is the most-skipped 5 seconds per photo and the highest-leverage one for S E O + AI search.
The phone version works in good light, the variable that matters most is time of day, not the sensor.
Re-shoot dates: Memorial Day prep, mid-October prep, plus any major menu change.
Take the spec to set.

The Photo Shot List sheet turns the spec into the day-of tool, dish × plate × garnish × props × channel target × aspect × priority × backup dish. Print it, bring it to set, tick each shot as it lands. The post tells you what to shoot; the sheet keeps the shoot from drifting.
